newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: More than 50,000 union workers rally in Seoul.
newsitem.headline: More than 50,000 union workers rally in Seoul.

text.p: Tens of thousands of South Korean workers rallied in Seoul on Sunday calling for a revision of restrictive labour laws and threatening all-out industrial action unless their demands are met.
Earlier, Labour Minister Jin Nyum had said the government would overhaul controversial legislation curbing labour union power by the end of this year.
His comments followed a meeting of senior government and ruling New Korea Party officials to discuss how to press ahead with legal revision.

A presidential commission formed in May has failed to produce a blueprint to bring South Korean labour practices into line with those of industrialised nations. Labour union representatives have pulled out of the body.
Witnesses said around 50,000 workers, many of them members of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, staged a rally on a vast concrete plaza near the National Assembly building.
Some wore headbands reading "Struggle for Democratic Revision of Labour Laws".
About 15,000 riot policemen ringed the rally site but no violence was reported.

Union anger is directed at laws that bar more than one union in each work place, prevent third-party intervention in industrial disputes and prohibit civil servants and all teachers from joining unions.
The Korean Confederation worries the government will shy away from wholesale reform for fear of offending big business groups, known as "chaebol".
Kwon Young-kil, president of the outlawed union, issued a warning to President Kim Young-sam against delaying revision of the laws, or even making them more restrictive.
If this happened, he told the rally "I solemly declare in the name of our 500,000 members that we would stage an all-out struggle, including a total strike".
Labour Minister Jin suggested the government would take over the work of the presidential commission, which dissolved amid acrimony between unionists and chaebol representatives.
He told reporters Sunday's meeting "agreed to recommend to the president that the government draw up its own draft bill and send it to the National Assembly at an early date".
Asked if there was a timetable he said "within this year".

South Korea is under pressure to liberalise its labour regulations as it prepares to join the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). It was invited into the Paris-based grouping in October.

Business leaders are opposed to giving unions more power at a time when they are cutting costs to cope with an economic downturn. Belt-tightening measures, including shedding staff and curbing wage increases, have alarmed workers and threaten industrial unrest.
Last week two Geneva-based union federations accused Seoul of backing away from labour reform and warned they would strive to block South Korea's admission to the OECD.
The white-collar Workers' Federation and International Metalworkers' Federation represent 30 million private-sector service workers and metalworkers around the world.
South Korea's tough labour laws are a legacy of past military-backed governments.
